page.h1: HTS Chapter 72: Iron and Steel — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: U.S. Steel & Scrap Export Rules: Schedule B, Licences, EEI & Drawback (HTS Ch. 72) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What U.S. exporters of steel, ferrous scrap and ferroalloys must do before shipping: Schedule B grades for scrap, the Russia licence rule, maraging-steel controls, EEI for bulk vessels, the Section 232 drawback bar and Canada surtax remission.
keywords: schedule b number for steel scrap

intro: A U.S. exporter of steel or ferrous scrap takes the same five steps as every exporter, and for most Chapter 72 goods that is all: nearly everything in the chapter is **EAR99** and needs no export licence. Three things are specific to this chapter. **Russia and Belarus:** every six-digit Chapter 72 code is on the Commerce sanctions list, so any shipment there needs a licence. **Maraging steel** is controlled for missile and nuclear reasons (ECCNs 1C116 and 1C216). And **drawback:** the 50% Section 232 duty paid on imported steel slabs, coils or bars cannot be refunded when the steel, or a product rolled from it, is exported. Scrap is excluded from federal hazardous-waste rules when it is recycled, so it needs no EPA export notice, but buyers in Türkiye, India, Bangladesh and other markets set their own inspection and radiation rules (see Markets).

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Ferrous scrap (7204) was a third of 2025 exports ($5.45B), and its Schedule B numbers split by grade: 7204.49.0020 No. 1 heavy melting, 7204.49.0040 No. 2 heavy melting, 7204.49.0060 cut plate and structural, 7204.49.0070 shredded and 7204.49.0080 other, with turnings and bundles in 7204.41 and stainless and alloy scrap in 7204.21 and 7204.29. Scrap is reported in metric tons. Flat steel splits by width (600 mm), rolling (hot or cold), coating and thickness, so check the exact line before quoting a buyer's tariff.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Scrap and commodity steel are often sold through trading houses and resold afloat, so screen the destination mill and final consignee, not only the trader on the contract.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Almost all Chapter 72 goods are EAR99. The exception is maraging steel (high-nickel, very low-carbon alloy steel, usually in 7225, 7226 or 7228): ECCN 1C116 covers grades with an ultimate tensile strength of at least 0.9 GPa solution-annealed or 1.5 GPa precipitation-hardened in sheet, plate or tube up to 5.0 mm thick (or large tubes), and ECCN 1C216 covers other maraging steel capable of 1,950 MPa, except forms with every dimension 75 mm or less. Maraging steel specially designed for uranium enrichment needs an NRC licence instead.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Russia and Belarus: all 167 six-digit Chapter 72 codes, from pig iron and ferroalloys to scrap and stainless wire, are listed in Supplement No. 4 to 15 CFR Part 746, so every Chapter 72 export to either country needs a Commerce licence. Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Syria are covered by country-wide rules.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Most scrap and much steel leaves by bulk vessel: file the EEI and give the carrier the ITN at least 24 hours before the cargo is loaded at the U.S. port, not at departure. Shipments to Canada are exempt from EEI unless a licence is needed; shipments to Mexico are not.

rules.title: Russia and Belarus: a licence is required for every Chapter 72 good — all 167 six-digit codes are in Supplement No. 4 to Part 746 (15 CFR 746.8(a)(5))

citations.label: Supplement No. 4 to Part 746 (industry sector list)

rules.agency: Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS); Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
rules.title: Maraging steel: ECCN 1C116 (missile technology and nuclear) and ECCN 1C216 (nuclear) need a licence for most destinations outside close allies; maraging steel designed for uranium isotope separation is licensed by the NRC (10 CFR Part 110)

citations.label: Commerce Control List, Category 1 (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1)

rules.title: Ferrous scrap being recycled is excluded (processed, home and prompt scrap) or exempt (other scrap metal) from hazardous-waste rules, so no EPA export notice or consent is needed; scrap mixed with hazardous waste such as batteries or PCB-containing parts is not covered

No drawback of the Section 232 duty on imported Chapter 72 steel articles, even when they or products made from them are exported (Proclamation 11021, clauses 13 and 14: manufacturing drawback is allowed only for certain derivative articles of trade-agreement partners); ordinary duties on the same entry can still be claimed

groups.label: Ferrous waste & scrap
groups.note: Scrap is not a Section 232 steel article, so drawback of any U.S. duty on imported scrap follows the normal rules. Foreign buyers often ask for a radiation-free certificate and pre-shipment inspection; those are their import rules (see Markets).

groups.label: Angles, shapes & sections
groups.note: Cold-formed shapes (7216.61–7216.91) are outside the Section 232 steel-article list, so their drawback follows the normal rules.

groups.label: Alloy flat steel (600 mm+)
groups.note: Maraging-steel sheet and plate falls here; ordinary alloy flat steel is EAR99.

groups.label: Alloy flat steel (under 600 mm)
groups.note: Maraging-steel strip falls here; ordinary alloy strip is EAR99.

groups.label: Alloy bars, shapes & drill rods
groups.note: Maraging-steel bars and forgings fall here; ordinary alloy bars are EAR99.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Help the Canadian buyer claim remission of Canada's steel surtax
savings.saves: Canada's 50% surtax on U.S. steel (7206–7229), refunded or waived when the goods qualify.
savings.appliesTo: Goods on Schedule 6 of Canada's United States Surtax Remission Order (2025), with no time limit: all stainless flat-rolled steel (7219, 7220), grain-oriented electrical steel (7225.11, 7226.11), other silicon-electrical steel (7225.19, 7226.19), high-speed steel strip (7226.20) and listed stainless and alloy bars and shapes; specific products and named importers listed in Schedules 2, 3 and 4.1; and steel imported from February 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 for making motor vehicles, vehicle parts or aircraft.
savings.document: A remission claim by the Canadian importer to the Canada Border Services Agency (for the Minister of Public Safety) within two years of import.
savings.caveat: The general remission for steel used in Canadian manufacturing ended for imports from February 1, 2026, so most carbon flat steel, rebar and wire rod now pays the full 50%. Only the Canadian importer can claim; the U.S. exporter helps by giving the exact tariff classification and end use.

citations.label: United States Surtax Remission Order (2025), SOR/2025-122 (consolidated)

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
